explanation: Additional authored interval text and highlighted events, preserved as source structures. Many are already applied to geologic_intervals.json.

paleocene.summary: Early Cenozoic recovery and diversification after the end-Cretaceous extinction.
paleocene.life: Mammalian and avian groups spread into ecological roles vacated by non-avian dinosaurs.

eocene.etym: Greek ēṓs “dawn” + kainós “recent”: dawn of many modern mammalian lineages.
eocene.summary: Extremely warm early Eocene conditions precede progressive cooling.
eocene.climate: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum occurs just before the Eocene; Early Eocene Climatic Optimum follows.
eocene.life: Early whales, horses, primates and many forest-associated mammals diversify.
events: ~56 Ma: rapid carbon injection and warming at PETM boundary

oligocene.etym: Greek olígos “few” + kainós “recent,” reflecting relatively few modern molluscan forms recognized in original classification.
oligocene.summary: Antarctic ice sheets and cooler climates restructure ecosystems.
oligocene.climate: Sharp cooling and Antarctic ice-sheet expansion near the epoch start.
oligocene.life: Open habitats become more widespread; mammalian faunas turn over.

miocene.etym: Greek meíōn “less” + kainós “recent,” based on proportions of living molluscan forms.
miocene.summary: Apes radiate, grassy ecosystems expand and modern oceanic currents develop.
miocene.climate: Middle Miocene warmth followed by cooling and increased aridity.
miocene.life: Ape diversity, grasses, grazing herbivores and marine mammals diversify.

pliocene.etym: Greek pleíōn “more” + kainós “recent,” reflecting the larger fraction of modern molluscs.
pliocene.summary: Cooling intensifies as ecosystems approach the ice-age world.
pliocene.climate: A generally warmer early Pliocene transitions toward Northern Hemisphere glaciation.
pliocene.life: Early hominins and increasingly modern mammal communities.

pleistocene.etym: Greek pleîstos “most” + kainós “recent,” indicating a very high proportion of modern molluscan species.
pleistocene.summary: Repeated glacial cycles and a remarkable megafauna accompany hominin expansion.
pleistocene.climate: Ice sheets wax and wane in repeated orbital-paced cycles.
pleistocene.life: Mammoths, saber-toothed cats, archaic humans and eventually Homo sapiens.

holocene.etym: Greek hólos “whole, entire” + kainós “recent,” meaning entirely recent.
holocene.summary: The current interglacial: agriculture, cities and large human environmental impacts.
holocene.climate: Relatively stable postglacial warmth compared with glacial–interglacial swings; recent anthropogenic warming.
holocene.life: Modern ecosystems under growing human influence.
events: ~12–10 ka: agriculture arises in several regions

earlycret.summary: Flowering plants first become conspicuous in the fossil record; many major dinosaur and bird lineages persist.

latecret.summary: Flowering plants radiate extensively; near the end, Chicxulub impact accompanies the K–Pg extinction.

latejur.summary: A famous interval for large sauropod faunas and Archaeopteryx.

earlytr.summary: Ecological recovery after the devastating end-Permian extinction.

latetr.summary: Dinosaurs and early mammaliaforms evolve as Pangaea starts to break apart.

lateord.summary: An end-Ordovician glaciation and extinction event strongly affect marine life.

latedev.summary: Early limbed vertebrates coexist with enormous reef systems before biotic crises.

mississippian.summary: Extensive shallow seas and diversified crinoids, with land forests advancing.

pennsylvanian.summary: Coal forests, early amniotes and diverse large arthropods populate equatorial wetlands.

danian.summary: Directly after the K–Pg mass extinction, mammal, bird and marine food webs reorganize.
events: Post-impact ecological recovery and new mammal radiations

ypresian.summary: Early Eocene greenhouse climates promote tropical and subtropical forests at high latitudes.
ypresian.climate: Some of the warmest sustained Cenozoic climates.

lutetian.summary: Early whales transition into more fully aquatic forms; warm forests persist.

rupelian.summary: After Eocene–Oligocene cooling, major ice expands on Antarctica.

messinian.summary: The Mediterranean undergoes the Messinian Salinity Crisis, producing thick evaporite deposits.
messinian.geo: Widespread Mediterranean evaporites from extreme basin restriction (~5.97–5.33 Ma).

zanclean.summary: Rapid refilling of the Mediterranean at the beginning of the Pliocene is a leading explanation for its re-connection to the Atlantic.

gelasian.summary: Quaternary glaciations intensify; large ice-age climate oscillations reshape habitats.

chibanian.summary: Middle Pleistocene glacial cycles and changing hominin communities.

upperpleist.summary: Anatomically modern humans spread globally; large mammals decline in many regions.

greenlandian.summary: Early Holocene warming follows the end of the Younger Dryas cold episode.

northgrippian.summary: Mid-Holocene civilizations and landscape changes unfold under relatively warm conditions.

meghalayan.summary: Late Holocene histories of agriculture, states, urbanization and industrialization.

aptian.summary: Diversifying flowering plants become clearer in terrestrial fossil assemblages.

cenomanian.summary: Warm seas and widespread marine ecosystems accompany elevated atmospheric CO₂.

maastrichtian.summary: The last age of non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites ends at the 66 Ma K–Pg extinction.
events: 66 Ma: Chicxulub impact; non-avian dinosaurs and ammonites become extinct

tithonian.summary: Early bird relatives and large theropod and sauropod faunas inhabit Late Jurassic ecosystems.

carnian.summary: The Carnian Pluvial Episode involves notable environmental disruptions; dinosaur diversification occurs across the Triassic.

changhsingian.summary: Massive environmental disruption culminates in the end-Permian extinction.

frasnian.summary: Kellwasser-related environmental disruptions contribute to Late Devonian marine extinctions.

hirnantian.summary: Rapid glaciation and sea-level change coincide with the end-Ordovician extinction.

fortunian.summary: Trace fossils signal increasing animal movement and sediment mixing in early Cambrian seas.

wuliuan.summary: Diverse Cambrian marine communities include spectacular soft-bodied fossil deposits.

insights.earth: Rock sequences, radiometric dating, fossils, isotopic proxies and plate reconstructions provide independent but uneven windows into Earth history.
insights.cambrian: Cambrian fossil lagerstätten reveal both mineralized shells and exceptional soft tissues; diversification was protracted rather than instantaneous.
insights.ordovician: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event transformed seafloor communities, followed by glaciation-linked marine extinctions.
insights.silurian: Recovery after Late Ordovician extinction coincided with expanding reef systems and early land-plant ecosystems.
insights.devonian: Reef systems, wooded floodplains and the fin-to-limb transition developed amid repeated ocean anoxic crises.
insights.carboniferous: Extensive tropical wetlands buried organic carbon and helped generate major coal deposits; early amniotes appeared.
insights.permian: Pangaea produced strong continental climate contrasts; end-Permian volcanism and biotic collapse fundamentally reorganized ecosystems.
insights.triassic: Life recovered and reorganized after the end-Permian crisis; the first dinosaurs and mammals arose in ecosystems with strong climatic seasonality.
insights.jurassic: Marine ammonites and reptilian predators flourished, while conifer forests supported sauropods and early feathered avialans.
insights.cretaceous: High sea levels flooded continents. Angiosperms diversified alongside pollinating insects; the interval ended at the K–Pg extinction.
insights.paleogene: Mammals and birds radiated after the K–Pg extinction; Eocene warmth preceded Oligocene Antarctic ice-sheet expansion.
insights.neogene: Expanding open habitats favored grazing mammals while tectonics reshaped ocean gateways and rainfall patterns.
insights.quaternary: Glacial–interglacial cycles strongly influenced sea level, biogeography and dispersal of Homo and associated megafaunas.
insights.cenozoic: Repeated climate transitions, Himalayan uplift and changing ocean gateways structured modern marine and terrestrial faunas.
